cards.explanation: The answer is a miserable task, friends. The Teacher says, “What a miserable task God has laid upon the sons of men to occupy them!” (Ecclesiastes 1:13) The Teacher, king in Jerusalem, sounds like a man who is nine hours into a job nobody warned him about. I think he's tired just thinking about it.

The picture is a pursuit of the wind, friends. The Teacher says he found it all to be “…futile, a pursuit of the wind.” Think about chasing the wind. You run, you reach, and your hands come back empty. I have chased a loose bit of parchment across a kitchen with a mustache, and the parchment won.

The answer is False, friends. The Teacher says the opposite. The text reads, “What is crooked cannot be straightened, and what is lacking cannot be counted.” Crooked stays crooked. Anyone who has watched a cookie come out of the oven shaped like a lopsided mitten knows the feeling.

The word is wisdom, friends. The Teacher tells himself, “…I have grown and increased in wisdom beyond all those before me who were over Jerusalem…” That is a king looking at his own brain and being impressed. I think he's feeling pretty good about himself right there.

The answer is much sorrow, friends. That's the reason the Teacher gives. He says, “For with much wisdom comes much sorrow, and as knowledge grows, grief increases.” The more he sees, the more it weighs on him. That's a heavy verse, so we let it sit for a second.

The answer is False, friends. After the Teacher tells himself, “enjoy what is good!” he says, “…it proved to be futile.” He tested pleasure honestly, and it didn't hold up. I'd say it's the saddest taste test in the book.

The answer is that it is folly, friends. The Teacher says of laughter, “It is folly…” and of pleasure, “What does it accomplish?” (Ecclesiastes 2:2). Now, I take laughter seriously around here, so I'm just reading you the verse and keeping my mustache folded.

The answer is True, friends. The Teacher says he sought to cheer his body with wine and to embrace folly, “…my mind still guiding me with wisdom…” So his head stayed in the driver's seat while he did it.

The answer is what is worth doing in life, friends. The Teacher keeps at it “…until I could see what was worthwhile for men to do under heaven during the few days of their lives.” He's not just having fun, he's hunting for something that's worth doing. And he says the days are few, so I think he doesn't want to waste them.

The answer is that he surpasses them all, friends. The text reads, “So I became great and surpassed all in Jerusalem who had preceded me; and my wisdom remained with me.” That includes everyone before him in Jerusalem. That's a whole line of people he left behind.

The answer is False, friends. The Teacher says, “Anything my eyes desired, I did not deny myself. I refused my heart no pleasure.” So he denied himself nothing his eyes desired. Me, I have to hide the cookie tin from myself.

The word is nothing, friends. The Teacher looks back at all he toiled to achieve and says, “there was nothing to be gained under the sun.” He had the houses, the gold and the gardens, and still he says that. That's a lot of work to end up with a verdict like that.
